blocks.content: When a process is loaded, or an already running process asks for more memory, the operating system has to decide exactly where in physical memory that request will live. Physical memory is limited and shared by everyone, so this decision, made over and over, shapes how well the whole system holds up over time.

This chapter walks through contiguous memory allocation, the classic version of that decision: the operating system tracks memory as a list of free and used blocks, and must pick a free block for every new request. It covers the three textbook strategies for making that pick, works one numeric example through all three so the difference is directly visible, and closes with fragmentation, coalescing, and why modern systems mostly moved on to paging instead.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408759737-902678202.png
1. The Memory Placement Problem

Every time a process is loaded into memory, or a running process calls something like malloc for more heap space, the operating system faces the same core question: where should this data actually go. Physical memory is a limited, shared resource with many processes competing for it at once, so the answer has to be found quickly, and it has to be found correctly, since two processes can never be given overlapping space.

This chapter focuses on one classic way of answering that question, called contiguous memory allocation. The operating system treats physical memory as one long sequence of blocks, and at any moment each block is either free (an unused hole) or used (currently occupied by some process). When a new request arrives, the operating system must choose one free block large enough to hold it, and if that block is bigger than the request needs, the extra space is split off and kept as a new, smaller free block.

blocks.title: In one sentence
blocks.content: Contiguous memory allocation is the problem of choosing which free block of physical memory should satisfy a new request, given a list of free and used blocks of varying sizes.
The free block list

To make this decision, the operating system keeps track of every free block in a structure usually called the free list. Each entry simply records where a hole begins and how big it is. Used blocks do not need the same bookkeeping for allocation purposes, since the allocator job is choosing among the holes, not the occupied space.

This list changes constantly. Every allocation shrinks a free block or removes it from the list entirely. Every time a process finishes and releases its memory, a new free block is added back in. The question this chapter is really about is which free block the operating system should pick whenever more than one of them is large enough to satisfy a request.

blocks.title: What happens to the leftover space
blocks.content: When an allocation is smaller than the free block it lands in, that block splits into two pieces: a used piece sized exactly to the request, and a new free piece covering whatever remains. That leftover piece goes straight back into the free list, so its size matters a great deal. A strategy that leaves a large, useful leftover behaves very differently over time than one that leaves a tiny, awkward sliver.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408863899-335515440.png
{"headers":["Block","Size","Status"],"rows":[["A","100 KB","Free"],["B","500 KB","Free"],["C","200 KB","Free"],["D","300 KB","Free"],["E","600 KB","Free"]]}

This is the running example used for the rest of the chapter. Picture these five holes sitting one after another in physical memory, from Block A to Block E in address order, and picture a new request for 212 KB that needs to be placed somewhere among them. The next three sections apply each strategy to exactly this scenario, so every difference between them is visible on the same numbers rather than three separate, incomparable examples.
2. First Fit

First fit is the simplest of the three strategies. The operating system scans the free list starting from the very beginning of memory, lowest address first, and allocates the very first block it finds that is large enough for the request. As soon as one qualifying block turns up, the search stops immediately, no matter how many other free blocks exist further along the list.

Because it stops at the first match, first fit is fast, often the fastest of the three strategies to compute, since it rarely needs to look at the whole free list. That speed has a cost that shows up later: the small blocks near the start of memory keep getting picked apart by many small requests, so over time they fragment into a cluster of tiny, unusable leftovers near the front of memory, even while plenty of usable space might exist further along.
Worked example

Apply first fit to the scenario from the table above with an incoming request of 212 KB. Block A is only 100 KB, too small, so it is skipped. Block B is 500 KB, which is large enough, so the search stops right there and Block B is chosen, even though Block D at 300 KB would have wasted less space. Blocks C, D, and E are never even examined, because first fit does not look any further once it finds a match.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408863901-826800880.png
First fit in code
3. Best Fit

Best fit takes the opposite approach to speed. Instead of stopping at the first match, it scans every single free block in the list and keeps track of the smallest one that is still large enough for the request. Only after checking every candidate does it make its final choice, picking whichever qualifying block wastes the least space.

The appeal is obvious: minimizing wasted space on each individual allocation sounds like the right goal. In practice, best fit tends to produce a large number of very small, nearly useless leftover fragments scattered throughout memory, because it deliberately hunts for the tightest possible fit every single time, and a tight fit by definition leaves only a sliver behind. Over many allocations, memory fills up with slivers too small to be useful for almost anything.
Worked example

Apply best fit to the same scenario and the same 212 KB request. Every block is checked: A at 100 KB and C at 200 KB are both too small to qualify. Among the blocks that do qualify, B at 500 KB, D at 300 KB, and E at 600 KB, the smallest is D at 300 KB, so best fit chooses Block D. The leftover after this allocation is only 88 KB, the tightest leftover of the three strategies for this request.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408863901-197401727.png
4. Worst Fit

Worst fit goes in the opposite direction entirely. It also scans every free block, but instead of picking the smallest qualifying one, it deliberately allocates the largest free block available in the entire list, regardless of how much bigger it is than the request actually needs.

The reasoning sounds sensible at first: if a big block is going to be split anyway, leaving behind a big leftover fragment seems more likely to be useful for some future request than leaving behind a tiny one. In practice this logic tends to backfire. Worst fit consumes the large blocks quickly, since every allocation chips away at whichever block happens to be biggest, and once the large blocks are gone, later requests that genuinely need a large contiguous block have nowhere left to go. Of the three strategies, worst fit is generally considered the weakest performer despite its seemingly reasonable logic.
Worked example

Apply worst fit to the same scenario and the same 212 KB request. Every block is checked, and the largest one overall is Block E at 600 KB, so worst fit chooses Block E regardless of how much better a fit some other block might have offered. The leftover after this allocation is 388 KB, by far the largest leftover of the three strategies for this request.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408863901-946180472.png
5. Comparing All Three on the Same Scenario
blocks.text: 5. Comparing All Three on the Same Scenario

blocks.content: The real value of walking through the same numbers three times is that the difference between the strategies becomes impossible to miss. Given the identical free list and the identical 212 KB request, each strategy lands on a different block, as the comparison below shows.

blocks.alt: Comparing All Three on the Same Scenario

blocks.content: Best fit produced the smallest leftover for this one allocation, which is exactly what it is designed to do. A single allocation only tells part of the story though. What matters over the life of a real system is what happens after hundreds or thousands of allocations and frees, and that is where the three strategies pull apart the most, as summarized below.

{"headers":["Strategy","Allocation speed","Memory utilization","Fragmentation tendency"],"rows":[["First fit","Fast, stops at the first match","Good on average","Small fragments accumulate near the start of memory"],["Best fit","Slow, must scan the entire free list","Best for any single allocation","Many tiny, scattered fragments build up over time"],["Worst fit","Slow, must scan the entire free list","Poor, wastes large blocks quickly","Runs out of large blocks for future big requests"]]}

First fit trades a little wasted space for speed and simplicity, best fit trades speed for a tighter individual fit that backfires into many small fragments, and worst fit gives up large blocks early in the hope that big leftovers stay useful later, a bet that rarely pays off.
6. Fragmentation and Coalescing

No matter which of the three strategies is used, contiguous memory allocation eventually runs into the same underlying problem: fragmentation. As processes come and go, allocating and freeing blocks of many different sizes, the free memory that remains gets chopped into smaller and smaller pieces, scattered across different addresses. Even when total free memory is large, no single free block may be big enough to satisfy a new large request, because that free memory is spread across many small, disconnected holes.

The earlier examples already show this in miniature. Best fit leaves tiny slivers behind on almost every allocation, and worst fit slowly erodes the large blocks that future big requests will need. Both patterns, repeated many times, are what fragmentation actually looks like in a running system.

blocks.title: Coming up in this module
blocks.content: Fragmentation gets its own dedicated topic in this module, covering internal versus external fragmentation and how each allocation strategy contributes to it in far more depth. Paging, the mechanism that largely sidesteps this entire class of problem, also has its own dedicated topic.
Coalescing: merging free neighbors

One straightforward mitigation is coalescing. Whenever a block of memory is freed, the operating system checks whether either of its immediate neighbors in memory is also free. If a neighbor is free, the two adjacent free blocks are merged into a single, larger free block, instead of being left as two smaller separate entries in the free list.

Coalescing does not eliminate fragmentation, since two small free blocks that sit apart in memory still cannot be merged with each other. What it does is prevent unnecessary fragmentation from building up simply because the operating system failed to notice that neighboring space was already free. Any allocator using contiguous allocation should coalesce on every free, as a matter of basic hygiene.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408863902-1047932.png
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408863902-208018119.png
7. Why Paging Replaced Pure Contiguous Allocation
blocks.text: 7. Why Paging Replaced Pure Contiguous Allocation

blocks.content: Everything covered so far assumes memory is handed out in variable sized, contiguous chunks, which is exactly what makes first fit, best fit, and worst fit meaningful choices in the first place. Modern general purpose operating systems mostly do not allocate physical memory this way anymore.

Once physical memory is divided into small, fixed size units called pages, and matching frames in physical memory, a request no longer needs one single contiguous hole big enough to hold it. It can be broken up and satisfied with any combination of free pages scattered anywhere in memory, because a layer of address translation stitches those scattered pages back into one continuous logical view for the process. That change makes the whole hunt for a right sized hole, and most of this chapter strategies, far less relevant in modern systems.

This is only a forward pointer for now. The dedicated Paging topic in this module explains exactly how fixed size pages and frames work, and why they sidestep contiguous allocation fragmentation problems almost entirely.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785408863902-737521713.png
blocks.alt: Why Paging Replaced Pure Contiguous Allocation

blocks.content: 8. Common Mistakes

The most common mistake is assuming that best fit must be the best overall choice simply because of its name. In practice it very often performs worse than first fit over the long run, precisely because its habit of choosing the tightest possible fit leaves behind a trail of tiny fragments that are too small to be useful for almost any future request.

A second common mistake is implementing an allocator that forgets to coalesce adjacent free blocks after memory is freed. Skipping that step quietly lets fragmentation accumulate far faster than it needs to, since perfectly mergeable neighboring space is left sitting as separate, smaller entries in the free list instead of being combined back into something useful.

["Do not assume best fit minimizes fragmentation just because it minimizes leftover space on a single allocation.","Always check both neighbors of a freed block and coalesce whenever either one is also free.","Remember all three strategies answer the same underlying question, which free block satisfies this request, they only differ in how they search and choose."]
items: Do not assume best fit minimizes fragmentation just because it minimizes leftover space on a single allocation.
Always check both neighbors of a freed block and coalesce whenever either one is also free.
Remember all three strategies answer the same underlying question, which free block satisfies this request, they only differ in how they search and choose.

blocks.content: 9. Interview Angle

Contiguous memory allocation is a favorite whiteboard question because it is small enough to work through by hand but rich enough to test real understanding. Interviewers often give a short list of free block sizes and one request size, then ask which block each of the three strategies would choose, exactly like the worked example earlier in this chapter.

The safest way to prepare is to practice tracing all three strategies by hand on a few made up scenarios until the mechanics feel automatic: scan and stop for first fit, scan everything and pick the smallest qualifying block for best fit, scan everything and pick the largest block for worst fit. Being able to explain, in one sentence each, why best fit is not automatically the best choice, and why worst fit tends to perform the worst, is usually what separates a memorized answer from real understanding.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.content: Be ready to trace first fit, best fit, and worst fit by hand on a small list of free blocks. This exact style of question shows up often, and being fast and accurate with it signals solid fundamentals.
